odessos.t: Milesian colony on the Bay of Varna that linked Thracian kingdoms to Aegean trade for five centuries and grew into modern Varna.
odessos.o: Odessos was founded by colonists from Miletus on the western Black Sea coast, usually dated to c. 585-570 BCE, at the mouth of a valley leading inland towards Thrace. The site had good anchorage and access to fertile land, and the colony grew through exchange with the Thracian Getae and Odrysians of the interior.
odessos.r: Odessos was a self-governing Greek polis whose prosperity rested on grain, fish, wine imports and trade with Thracian rulers, whose wealth appears in rich local tombs. Its chief deity was the Great God, a Hellenised form of the Thracian Darzalas, shown on its coins. Under Lysimachus it joined a revolt of the Pontic cities in 313 BCE.
odessos.e: Like Tomis, Callatis and Mesembria, Odessos came under Roman control after the campaign of Marcus Terentius Varro Lucullus in 72-71 BCE. As Odessus it prospered in the Roman province of Moesia, with large public baths, and later passed to Byzantium and the Bulgarians. The modern city is Varna.
odessos.re: Ancient Greek religion (cult of the Great God)

ostrogothic-kingdom.t: Gothic kingdom of Theodoric the Great in Italy, which preserved Roman government and culture before Justinian's armies destroyed it.
ostrogothic-kingdom.o: The Ostrogoths, settled in the Balkans as federates of the eastern empire, were sent to Italy by the emperor Zeno under their king Theodoric. They invaded in 489, besieged Odoacer in Ravenna and killed him in 493, and Theodoric became ruler of Italy under nominal imperial authority.
ostrogothic-kingdom.r: Theodoric governed through Roman officials and the Senate, while the Goths formed the army and kept their Arian faith. Romans such as Cassiodorus and Boethius served him, though he executed Boethius in 524. Ravenna gained Sant'Apollinare Nuovo and his mausoleum. His realm reached into Provence, Dalmatia and the Alps, and he led a network of Germanic kingdoms through marriage alliances.
ostrogothic-kingdom.e: After Theodoric's death in 526, the murder of his daughter Amalasuntha gave Justinian a pretext to invade in 535. Belisarius and Narses fought the Goths for almost twenty years, leaving Italy devastated. Totila was killed at Busta Gallorum in 552, and Teia at Mons Lactarius in 552 or 553.

opuntian-locris.t: Confederation of the eastern Locrians on the Euboean Gulf, centred on Opus and remembered for the Locrian maidens sent to Troy.
opuntian-locris.o: The eastern Locrians lived along the coast of central Greece facing Euboea, separated from their western kin in Ozolian Locris by Doris and Phocis. Homer placed Ajax the Lesser among them. By the Archaic period their towns formed a confederation led by Opus, governed by an oligarchic council of a thousand.
opuntian-locris.r: The Locrians kept old customs, such as sending two noble maidens each year to serve Athena at Ilion in atonement for Ajax's sacrilege. An early 5th century BCE bronze tablet records the terms for Locrian colonists at Naupactus. They fought with Leonidas at Thermopylae in 480 BCE, then were forced to join the Persians, and later usually sided with Thebes and Sparta against Athens.
opuntian-locris.e: The Phocian League overran much of the region in the Third Sacred War. Eastern Locris later passed under Macedonian, Boeotian and Aetolian League control and came under Rome in 146 BCE.

olbia.t: Milesian colony on the Bug-Dnieper estuary that was the main Greek gateway to the Scythians, described first-hand by Herodotus.
olbia.o: Greeks from Miletus first settled on Berezan island in the 7th century BCE, and around 550 BCE founded Olbia ('the prosperous') on the right bank of the Hypanis (Southern Bug) estuary. Its people also called it Borysthenes, after the Dnieper. The colony took over much of the fertile surrounding steppe edge.
olbia.r: Olbia traded wine, olive oil and fine pottery to the Scythians for grain, fish, hides and slaves, and lived alongside Scythian rulers, one of whom, Scyles, kept a house there. A self-governing polis, it worshipped Apollo Delphinios and Achilles, and issued early cast bronze money shaped like dolphins. Herodotus visited in the 5th century BCE.
olbia.e: Olbia resisted a siege by Alexander's general Zopyrion c. 331 BCE but declined in the later Hellenistic period. Around 55 BCE the Getae under Burebista sacked it. It was later rebuilt on a smaller scale under Roman protection and abandoned in the 4th century CE. The ruins near Parutyne in Ukraine are a protected reserve.

orchomenus-boeotia.t: Ancient Boeotian city, heir of Mycenaean Orchomenos, which rivalled Thebes for leadership of Boeotia until the Thebans destroyed it in 364 BCE.
orchomenus-boeotia.o: After the collapse of the Mycenaean Kingdom of Orchomenos c. 1200 BCE, the town survived beside the refilled Lake Copais. In the Iron Age it became a Boeotian polis and the main rival of Thebes, sometimes leading western Boeotia. Its cult of the Graces, the Charites, was among the oldest in Greece.
orchomenus-boeotia.r: Orchomenus was a member of the Boeotian League and an oligarchy of landowners. It sided with Sparta against Thebes in the early 4th century BCE and fought at Coronea in 394 BCE. Its festival of the Charitesia attracted poets and musicians, and Pindar wrote an ode for an Orchomenian victor.
orchomenus-boeotia.e: Thebes destroyed Orchomenus in 364 BCE, killing its men. Philip II rebuilt it after Chaeronea in 338 BCE. Sulla defeated Mithridates's army nearby in 85 BCE, and the town, under Rome from 146 BCE, continued on a smaller scale.
orchomenus-boeotia.re: Greek religion; cult of the Charites

old-swiss-confederacy.t: The loose alliance of Alpine cantons that grew from a 1291 pact into a neutral federation of thirteen members, the forerunner of modern Switzerland.
old-swiss-confederacy.o: Tradition dates the Confederacy to the Federal Charter of August 1291, a defensive pact between Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden against outside lords, above all the Habsburgs. Victories at Morgarten in 1315, Sempach in 1386 and Näfels in 1388 drew in Lucerne, Zürich, Glarus, Zug and Bern, and by 1513 the alliance numbered thirteen cantons.
old-swiss-confederacy.r: There was no central government. The cantons, a mix of rural assemblies and patrician city republics, sent envoys to the Diet (Tagsatzung), which decided only by consensus. They jointly ruled subject territories and kept associates such as the Three Leagues and the Republic of Geneva. Swiss pikemen were Europe's most sought-after mercenaries, and the Reformation split the cantons into Catholic and Reformed camps that fought several civil wars.
old-swiss-confederacy.e: Independence from the Holy Roman Empire was recognised at the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. In 1798 French armies invaded and replaced the old order with the centralised Helvetic Republic. Napoleon's Act of Mediation of 1803 restored a federation, from which the modern Swiss state developed.

oxybii.t: Ligurian people of the coast near Fréjus who, with the Deciates, provoked Rome's first intervention beyond the Alps in 154 BCE.
oxybii.o: Known chiefly from Polybius, the Oxybii lived on the coast west of Antibes, near the port of Aegitna, probably around modern Mandelieu or Cannes.
oxybii.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers. Polybius tells that they attacked Roman envoys landing at Aegitna and wounded one of them.
oxybii.e: In 154 BCE the consul Quintus Opimius marched against them, took Aegitna and defeated them and the Deciates. Their land was given to Massalia and later absorbed into Gallia Narbonensis, where the Roman colony of Forum Julii (Fréjus) was founded nearby.

olynthus.t: Chief city of Chalcidice, head of the Chalcidian League, whose destruction by Philip II in 348 BCE left the best-preserved classical Greek town plan.
olynthus.o: Olynthus stood on hills near the head of the Toronaic Gulf. It was a town of the Bottiaeans until 479 BCE, when the Persian commander Artabazus massacred its people and handed it to Chalcidian Greeks under Critobulus of Torone. In 432 BCE many Chalcidians abandoned their coastal towns to settle there, at the urging of Perdiccas II of Macedon.
olynthus.r: Olynthus became the centre of the Chalcidian League, a federal state with shared citizenship and coinage of fine silver. A new town on a regular grid of blocks was built on the North Hill; excavations led by David Robinson in the 1920s and 1930s uncovered whole houses with courtyards, mosaics and household goods, a rich picture of daily life.
olynthus.e: Sparta forced the league to submit after a war in 382-379 BCE. Restored, Olynthus became Philip II's main rival in the north. Despite Demosthenes' Olynthiac speeches urging Athenian help, Philip took the city by treachery in 348 BCE, razed it and sold its people into slavery.

obotrite-confederation.t: A union of Slavic tribes in Mecklenburg whose princes alternated between alliance and war with Franks, Danes and Saxons, founding Mecklenburg's ruling house.
obotrite-confederation.o: The Obotrites (Abodrites) were West Slavic tribes who settled the coastlands of Mecklenburg and Holstein from the 7th century. From around 780 they appear as allies of Charlemagne against the Saxons, and their prince Drasco helped defeat the Nordalbingian Saxons in 798.
obotrite-confederation.r: The confederation united several tribes, including the Wagrians and Polabians, under princes with strongholds such as Mecklenburg near Wismar and Starigard (Oldenburg in Holstein). Trade passed through the port of Reric until the Danish king Godfred destroyed it in 808. Princes Gottschalk and Henry tried to Christianise the realm; a pagan revolt in 1066 killed Gottschalk.
obotrite-confederation.e: The Wendish Crusade of 1147 and the campaigns of Henry the Lion broke Obotrite power; Prince Niklot was killed in 1160. His son Pribislav accepted Saxon overlordship and Christianity in 1167, founding the Lordship of Mecklenburg, whose dynasty ruled until 1918.

ordovices.t: Mountain peoples of north-west Wales who hosted Caratacus' last stand and fought Rome until Agricola crushed them in 77 or 78.
ordovices.o: The Ordovices held the uplands of Snowdonia and much of mid and north Wales, a region of small hillforts, stone-walled roundhouses and pastoral farming. They enter written history through Tacitus, who records that the British leader Caratacus moved his war against Rome into their territory around 51 after leaving the Silures.
ordovices.r: No coins, kings or towns are known, and power was probably held by local chiefs controlling upland grazing and fortified settlements. Anglesey, the island of Mona, lay on their borders and was a centre of the druids, whose sanctuary Suetonius Paulinus attacked in 60 before Boudica's revolt recalled him. Their resistance made the region one of the last parts of Wales to be pacified.
ordovices.e: Around 77 the Ordovices destroyed a Roman cavalry unit. The new governor Agricola answered with a campaign that, Tacitus says, nearly wiped out the people, and then seized Anglesey. Their land was held by forts such as Segontium at Caernarfon, and no civitas of the Ordovices is known in Roman Britain.

odrysian-kingdom.t: The strongest Thracian state, a kingdom stretching from the Aegean to the Danube whose rich tombs and Greek-style city of Seuthopolis survive in Bulgaria.
odrysian-kingdom.o: Around 480 BCE, after the Persian retreat from Europe, Teres I united Thracian tribes of the Hebrus (Maritsa) valley under the Odrysians. His son Sitalces extended rule from Abdera on the Aegean to the Danube and allied with Athens at the start of the Peloponnesian War.
odrysian-kingdom.r: The king ruled through relatives and tribal princes, drawing tribute from Thracian tribes and Greek coastal cities; Thucydides valued the yearly income at some 400 talents. Gold and silver vessels such as the Panagyurishte and Rogozen treasures show elite wealth. Cotys I strengthened the crown in the 4th century, and Seuthes III built Seuthopolis near Kazanlak, where painted tombs survive.
odrysian-kingdom.e: Philip II of Macedon conquered much of the kingdom after 342 BCE. Odrysian rulers revived under Macedonian and then Roman overlordship as client kings. In 46 CE, after the murder of Rhoemetalces III, Claudius annexed the realm as the province of Thrace.

organisation-of-western-continental-gree.t: Regional revolutionary government of western mainland Greece in 1821-1822, organised by Alexandros Mavrokordatos at Missolonghi.
organisation-of-western-continental-gree.o: Western mainland Greece, from the Gulf of Corinth to Epirus, rose against the Ottomans in the spring of 1821. In November 1821 the Phanariot politician Alexandros Mavrokordatos gathered local representatives at Missolonghi, where they adopted a charter and created a senate to govern the region and coordinate the military chieftains.
organisation-of-western-continental-gree.r: The organisation had a senate of local notables and military leaders, with Mavrokordatos as president. It raised revenue, supplied armed bands and tried to restrain the chieftains, many of whom had served as armatoloi under the Ottomans. Missolonghi, a lagoon town, became the region's centre and later the scene of famous sieges.
organisation-of-western-continental-gree.e: With the First National Assembly at Epidaurus in January 1822 and the founding of the First Hellenic Republic, regional bodies were placed under the central government and were abolished during 1822. Mavrokordatos became president of the national executive.

oretani.t: An Iberian people of the upper Guadalquivir whose city Castulo controlled the silver mines of the Sierra Morena and gave Hannibal his wife.
oretani.o: The Oretani lived in the upper Guadalquivir valley and the southern Meseta, in modern Jaén and Ciudad Real, from the mid-first millennium BCE. They took their name from the town of Oretum, but their leading city was Castulo near Linares, a crossroads between the coast and the interior.
oretani.r: Their wealth came from the silver and lead mines of the Sierra Morena, exploited intensively under Carthaginian and then Roman control. Castulo had rich princely tombs and later minted bronze coins with an Iberian legend. Hannibal married Himilce, said to be a princess of Castulo, tying the Oretani to Barcid Iberia.
oretani.e: In 206 BCE Castulo went over to Rome during the Scipionic campaigns. The Oretani joined the revolt of 197 BCE but were absorbed into Hispania Citerior and later Tarraconensis, and Castulo remained an important Roman mining town.

ozolian-locris.t: Confederation of the western Locrians on the Gulf of Corinth, centred on Amphissa, whose clash with the Amphictyony brought Philip II into central Greece.
ozolian-locris.o: The western or Ozolian Locrians lived on the northern shore of the Gulf of Corinth, west of Delphi, in small hill towns such as Amphissa, Chaleion and Oeanthea. They were related to the Locrians of Opuntian Locris but separated by Phocis and Doris. Naupactus was theirs until Athens gave it to Messenian refugees c. 456 BCE.
ozolian-locris.r: Thucydides described the western Locrians as still carrying arms in daily life, a sign of archaic customs. Their towns were loosely confederated, with Amphissa the most important. A bronze tablet from Chaleion of the 5th century BCE regulates disputes between towns, a rare early example of Greek inter-state law.
ozolian-locris.e: When Amphissa farmed the sacred plain of Delphi, the Amphictyony declared the Fourth Sacred War; Philip II destroyed Amphissa in 338 BCE. Western Locris later joined the Aetolian League and came under Rome in 146 BCE.

osismii.t: Gallic people of the far western tip of Brittany, the end of the known world for Greek and Roman geographers.
osismii.o: The Osismii lived in Finistère and western Côtes-d'Armor. The Greek explorer Pytheas probably referred to them as the Ostimioi around 320 BCE, placing them on a promontory facing the Ocean. Caesar lists them among the Armorican peoples.
osismii.r: Their economy rested on farming, fishing and sea trade along the Atlantic route to Britain. No ruler or central town is recorded before the conquest.
osismii.e: They submitted to Publius Crassus in 57 BCE and supported the Veneti in 56 BCE. Under Rome their capital was Vorgium (Carhaix). In late antiquity their land was settled by migrants from Britain and became part of Domnonée and Cornouaille.

orchomenus-arcadia.t: Ancient hill city of northern Arcadia, a rival of Mantinea that refused to join the Arcadian League.
orchomenus-arcadia.o: Orchomenus occupied a hill between two upland plains in northern Arcadia. Tradition made it the seat of early Arcadian kings; the last, Aristocrates, was said to have been stoned for betraying the Messenians to Sparta in the 7th century BCE. Homer called it 'rich in flocks'.
orchomenus-arcadia.r: Orchomenus was an ally of Sparta in the Peloponnesian League and a rival of Mantinea, with which it fought over land and leadership in Arcadia. It sent troops to Thermopylae and Plataea. In 370 BCE it refused to join the new Arcadian League dominated by Mantinea and Tegea.
orchomenus-arcadia.e: In the Hellenistic period Orchomenus was taken in turn by the Aetolian League, Sparta and the Achaean League, and Antigonus Doson of the Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia captured it in 223 BCE. It passed under Rome in 146 BCE.

olcades.t: A people of the southern Meseta whose capital Althaia was Hannibal's first conquest as commander in Iberia, in 221 BCE.
olcades.o: The Olcades lived in the upper Guadiana and Júcar region of the southern Meseta, probably in modern Cuenca and Ciudad Real. Their origins are obscure, and ancient sources mention them only in connection with the Carthaginian campaigns.
olcades.r: Nothing is known of their institutions beyond their capital, which Polybius calls Althaia and Livy Cartala, and their wealth in cattle and grain.
olcades.e: In 221 BCE Hannibal attacked them, took Althaia and forced them to pay tribute. The next year Olcadian refugees joined the Carpetani and Vaccaei against him at the Tagus and were defeated. They vanish from the record after this, absorbed into Barcid Iberia and later Roman Hispania.
